claim: OrgC is encoded within the S. Typhimurium pathogenicity island 1 (SPI-1) T3SS gene cluster
source: OrgC (oxygen regulated gene C) is encoded within and co-regulated with the cluster of genes that encode the core components of the S. Typhimurium T3SS located within the pathogenicity island 1 (SPI-1) (Figure 1A) (Jones and Falkow, 1994; Klein et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript directly states that OrgC is encoded within SPI-1 and cites prior literature (Jones and Falkow, 1994; Klein et al., 2000).

claim: OrgC is secreted by the SPI-1 T3SS
source: Previous studies have shown that OrgC is secreted by the SPI-1 T3SS and since it was reported to be non-essential for type III secretion function, it was hypothesized to be an effector protein of this system (Aguirre et al., 2006; Day and Lee, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies (Aguirre et al., 2006; Day and Lee, 2003) that demonstrated OrgC secretion by the SPI-1 T3SS.

claim: OrgC translocation into host cells could not be detected
source: However, its translocation into host cells could not be detected (Day and Lee, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study (Day and Lee, 2003) that failed to detect OrgC translocation into host cells.

claim: Homologs of OrgC are encoded within T3SS gene clusters in several bacterial species
source: Homologs of OrgC encoded within T3SS gene clusters with high degree of synteny can be detected in several bacterial species (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting a potentially conserved function in type III secretion.
evidence: The manuscript presents sequence alignment data (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing OrgC homologs in multiple bacterial species.

claim: OrgC is an early substrate of the SPI-1 T3SS
source: Importantly, we found that OrgC is also secreted in the ∆invJ (Figure 1C) or spaSN258A (Figure 1D) mutant strains, indicating that it is an early substrate of the SPI-1 T3SS.
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot data (Figure 1C and 1D) showing OrgC secretion in mutant strains that only secrete early substrates.

claim: Early substrates are not injected into target host cells
source: As early substrates are not injected into target host cells, these observations are consistent with previous reports failed to detect the translocation of OrgC into mammalian cells (Day and Lee, 2003), and suggest that it may be involved in the assembly of the secretion machine.
evidence: The manuscript draws on established knowledge about early substrates and cites prior work (Day and Lee, 2003) to support the interpretation.

claim: The ∆orgC mutant exhibits reduced secretion of middle and late substrates
source: We found that the ∆orgC mutant exhibited reduced secretion of middle (i. e. SipB) and late (i. e. SptP) substrates (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot data (Figure 2A and B) showing reduced secretion of SipB and SptP in the ∆orgC mutant.

claim: The ∆orgC mutant exhibits significantly increased secretion of needle and inner rod subunit proteins PrgI and PrgJ
source: Notably, the ∆orgC mutant exhibited significantly increased level of secretion of the needle and inner rod subunit proteins PrgI and PrgJ.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations from secretion assays shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Secretion of middle and late substrates requires substrate switching, which can only occur upon completion of the needle filament and its subsequent attachment to the inner rod
source: These observations suggest that the ∆orgC mutant must have a defect in needle or inner rod assembly because secretion of middle and late substrates requires substrate switching, which can only occur upon completion of the needle filament and its subsequent attachment to the inner rod (Lefebre and Galán, 2014; Marlovits et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies (Lefebre and Galán, 2014; Marlovits et al., 2006) that established the requirement for needle completion before substrate switching.

claim: Deletion of orgC completely abolished the ∆invJ S. Typhimurium cell clumping
source: We found that the deletion of orgC completely abolished the ∆invJ S. Typhimurium cell clumping (Figure 2C) even though it did not alter the levels of the core components of the T3SS NC (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from a bacterial clumping assay (Figure 2C) and Western blot analysis (Figure 2D).

claim: Very few longer needles were observed on the surface of the S. Typhimurium ∆orgC ∆invJ mutant by electron microscopy
source: Consistent with this hypothesis and in sharp contrast with the ∆invJ mutant, very few longer needles were observed on the surface of the S. Typhimurium ∆orgC ∆invJ mutant when examined by electron microscopy (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy images (Figure 2E) showing the absence of long needles in the double mutant.

claim: The proportion of fully assembled NCs was significantly reduced in the S. Typhimurium ∆orgC mutant
source: We found that the proportion of fully assembled NCs (i. e. NC bases with needle substructures) vs. NCs without needle substructures was significantly reduced in the S. Typhimurium ∆orgC mutant (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy data (Figure 2F and G) quantifying the proportion of NCs with needles.

claim: The average length of the needles and the distribution of needle lengths in fully assembled NCs were indistinguishable between wild type and ∆orgC strains
source: However, both the average length of the needles and the distribution of needle lengths in fully assembled NCs were indistinguishable in both strains (Figure 2H).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data on needle length distribution (Figure 2H) comparing wild type and ∆orgC mutant.

claim: OrgC plays a role in the initiation of needle assembly but does not influence needle elongation or needle length
source: Taken together, these results indicate that OrgC plays a role in the initiation of needle assembly but does not influence needle elongation or needle length.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from multiple experimental observations including NC analysis and needle length measurements.

claim: Type III secretion machines recognize substrates through signals located at their amino termini
source: It is well established that type III secretion machines recognize substrates through signals located at their amino termini (Michiels and Cornelis, 1991; Sory and Cornelis, 1994; Rüssmann et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature (Michiels and Cornelis, 1991; Sory and Cornelis, 1994; Rüssmann et al., 2002) on T3SS substrate recognition.

claim: OrgC lacking its first 21 amino acids is not secreted
source: Both mutant constructs were stably expressed in a S. Typhimurium ∆orgC mutant strain but, in contrast to wild type OrgC, they were not detected in the culture supernatants indicating that their secretion was abolished (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot data (Figure 3A and B) showing absence of the mutant proteins in culture supernatants.

claim: MBP-tagged OrgC at the amino terminus is not secreted
source: In addition, we constructed a mutant in which a maltose-binding protein (MBP) tag was placed at the amino terminus of OrgC, an arrangement that interferes with type III protein secretion (Kubori and Galán, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript describes the construction of MBP-OrgC and cites prior work (Kubori and Galán, 2002) showing that N-terminal MBP tags interfere with T3SS secretion.

claim: Non-secretable forms of OrgC cannot complement the ∆orgC mutant
source: We found that although introduction of a plasmid encoding wild type OrgC was able to complement the clumping phenotype of the S. Typhimurium ∆orgC ∆invJ mutant, plasmids encoding either of the non-secreted forms of OrgC did not (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from bacterial clumping assays (Figure 3C) comparing wild type and mutant OrgC.

claim: OrgC secretion is necessary for its function
source: These results indicate that OrgC secretion is necessary for its function.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from experiments showing non-secreted OrgC mutants cannot complement the ∆orgC phenotype.

claim: Exogenous addition of purified OrgC can complement the clumping phenotype of a ∆orgC ∆invJ S. Typhimurium mutant
source: We found that addition of purified OrgC to cultures of the S. Typhimurium ∆invJ ∆orgC strain resulted in bacterial cell clumping (Figure 4A and B) indicating that OrgC is capable of complementing the ∆orgC mutant when exogenously applied.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from bacterial clumping assays (Figure 4A and B) with exogenously added purified OrgC.

claim: Exogenous OrgC-induced bacterial cell clumping is dependent on the presence of the ∆invJ mutation
source: The bacterial cell clumping observed was dependent on the presence of the ∆invJ mutation since exogenous addition of the OrgC protein did not induce clumping in the wild type strain or in a the ∆orgC mutant alone (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from bacterial clumping assays (Figure 4C) showing specificity of the OrgC effect.

claim: Exogenous OrgC-induced clumping is strictly dependent on the presence of the needle protein PrgI and a functional T3SS
source: Furthermore, the clumping was also strictly dependent on the presence of the needle protein PrgI and a functional T3SS since addition of the OrgC protein did not induce clumping in a ∆invJ/∆orgC/∆prgI, ∆invJ/∆orgC/∆invA, or ∆invJ/∆orgC/∆invG mutant strains (Figure 4D), which lack the needle substructure and/or are defective for type III secretion (Sukhan et al., 2001; Collazo and Galán, 1996; Galán et al., 1992; Kaniga et al., 1994).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from bacterial clumping assays (Figure 4D) with various mutant strains and cites prior work characterizing these mutants.

claim: Growth of the S. typhimurium ∆orgC mutant in the presence of purified OrgC resulted in decreased levels of the early substrate protein InvJ in the cultured supernatants
source: We also found that growth of the S. typhimurium ∆orgC mutant in the presence of purified OrgC resulted in decreased levels of the early substrate protein InvJ in the cultured supernatants (Figure 4E), which is consistent with the observed presence of a larger number of fully assembled NC in the presence of OrgC and presumably a more efficient substrate switching (see Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot data (Figure 4E) showing reduced InvJ secretion when OrgC is added exogenously.

claim: Abundant long needle structures were observed on the surface of the S. Typhimurium ∆invJ ∆orgC mutant when grown in the presence of OrgC but not in its absence
source: We found the presence of abundant long needle structures protruding from the surface of the mutant strain when grown in the presence of OrgC but not when grown in its absence (Figure 4F), despite the presence of equal levels of the components of the NC after growth under either condition (Figure 4G).
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy images (Figure 4F) and Western blot data (Figure 4G) comparing bacteria grown with and without OrgC.

claim: The proportion of fully assembled NCs was increased when the ∆orgC mutant was grown in the presence of purified OrgC protein
source: We found that the proportion of fully assembled NCs (i. e. NC bases with needle substructures) vs. NCs without needle substructures was increased when the ∆orgC mutant was grown in the presence of the purified OrgC protein (Figure 4H and I).
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy data (Figure 4H and I) quantifying NC assembly with and without exogenous OrgC.

claim: OrgC can stimulate needle assembly when exogenously applied to culture cells
source: Taken together, these results indicate that OrgC can stimulate needle assembly when exogenously applied to culture cells and suggest that OrgC must exert its function at a location within the needle complex that is accessible from the outside.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from multiple experiments showing exogenous OrgC can complement the ∆orgC phenotype.

claim: OrgC interacts with PrgI in S. Typhimurium cells
source: Using an affinity purification assay with a tagged version of OrgC we detected the interaction of OrgC with PrgI but not with the other type III secretion early substrates PrgJ and InvJ (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript presents co-immunoprecipitation data (Figure 5A) showing OrgC-PrgI interaction.

claim: The interaction between OrgC and PrgI is direct
source: Using this approach we readily detected the interaction between OrgC and PrgI∆C5 (Figure 5B), a mutant that lacks its last five residues and consequently is unable to polymerize thus preventing protein agregation (Poyraz et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript presents bacterial two-hybrid data (Figure 5B) demonstrating direct interaction and cites prior work (Poyraz et al., 2010) characterizing the PrgI mutant.

claim: Overexpression of PrgI suppresses the ∆orgC phenotype
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, when prgI was over-expressed in a ∆invJ ∆orgC background, the cell clumping was recovered despite the absence of OrgC (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from bacterial clumping assays (Figure 5C) showing PrgI overexpression can bypass the need for OrgC.

claim: OrgC significantly accelerates the polymerization of PrgI into needle filaments in vitro
source: We found that OrgC significantly accelerated the polymerization of PrgI into needle filaments (Figure 5D). Under the assay conditions used, recombinant PrgI polymerized into needles at about 120 min after initiation of the reaction. In contrast, in the presence of recombinant OrgC, PrgI polymerization could be detected as early as 30 min after initiation of the reaction (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript presents dynamic light scattering data (Figure 5D) showing accelerated PrgI polymerization in the presence of OrgC.

claim: OrgC directly facilitates the assembly of the PrgI needle filaments
source: Taken together, these results indicate that OrgC directly facilitates the assembly of the PrgI needle filaments.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from multiple experiments including co-IP, two-hybrid, and DLS assays.

claim: NMR titrations show direct and specific protein-protein interaction between OrgC and PrgI
source: Titrations of OrgC with PrgI showed direct and specific protein-protein interaction between OrgC and PrgI (Figure 6A–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents NMR spectroscopy data (Figure 6A-D and supplement) showing chemical shift changes upon titration.

claim: The primary sites of interaction involve OrgC residues 134–141 at the C-terminal region and PrgI residues K37, S39, Q48, and K66
source: The primary sites of interaction involved the OrgC residues 134–141 at the C-terminal region, and the PrgI residues K37, S39, Q48, and K66 at the head group of the alpha-helical hairpin and the C-terminal helix of PrgI (Figure 6A–6E).
evidence: The manuscript presents NMR data (Figure 6A-6E) identifying specific residues showing largest chemical shift changes.

claim: The interaction between OrgC and PrgI occurs at fast exchange NMR time scale, suggestive of weak binding with micromolar binding affinities
source: The change in peak positions during the titration indicated that the interaction occurred at fast exchange NMR time scale, which is suggestive of weak binding interaction typically seen for binding interactions with micromolar binding affinities.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the NMR data based on established principles of NMR spectroscopy.

claim: Amino acids involved in OrgC binding show higher conservation in needle filament proteins from T3SSs that have homologs of OrgC
source: Interestingly, amino acid sequence comparison of needle filament proteins showed a higher degree of conservation of amino acids involved in OrgC binding in the T3SSs that have homologs of OrgC relative to needle filament proteins from those that do not (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents sequence alignment data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) comparing needle proteins from different bacteria.

claim: Small deletions (∆134–136 and ∆137–140) within the predicted PrgI-binding site of OrgC abolished its ability to complement bacterial cell clumping
source: Introduction of small deletions (∆134–136 and ∆137–140) within the predicted PrgI-binding site of OrgC abolished its ability to complement bacterial cell clumping of a ∆orgC ∆invJ mutant strain (Figure 6F), even though introduction of the mutations did not affect the stability of OrgC (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from bacterial clumping assays (Figure 6F) and Western blots (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) with OrgC deletion mutants.

claim: Introduction of mutations in PrgI residues Q48, S52 and N55 reduced PrgI-mediated bacterial cell clumping
source: Similarly, introduction of mutations in the PrgI residues that showed significant changes in the NMR peak positions (Q48, S52 and N55) during the titration of OrgC reduced PrgI-mediated bacterial cell clumping (Figure 6F).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from bacterial clumping assays (Figure 6F) with PrgI mutants.

claim: The interaction of OrgC with PrgI is essential for its function
source: Taken together, these results validate the NMR titration experiments and demonstrate that the interaction of OrgC with PrgI is essential for its function.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from mutagenesis experiments targeting the OrgC-PrgI interface.

claim: The 3D structure of OrgC was determined by NMR methods
source: Therefore, we determined the 3D structure of OrgC by NMR methods.
evidence: The manuscript describes the NMR structure determination process and presents the resulting structure.

claim: Full-length recombinant OrgC expressed poorly, showed poor solubility, and produced poor quality NMR spectra
source: Full-length recombinant OrgC expressed poorly, showed poor solubility in NMR solution conditions, and the quality of NMR spectra showed poor resolution and heterogeneity in peak intensities suggestive of non-uniform protein conformations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations from NMR spectroscopy (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: The truncated form of OrgC (lacking first 20 amino acids) showed excellent quality of NMR spectra
source: The truncated form of OrgC showed excellent quality of NMR spectra (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) with well-resolved peaks of homogenous intensities that enabled the NMR structure determination.
evidence: The manuscript presents NMR spectra (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) comparing full-length and truncated OrgC.

claim: The overall structure of OrgC comprises a central region with four helices
source: The overall structure of OrgC comprises a central region with four helices – helix α1 (residues 46–57), helix α2 (residues 55–78), helix α3 (residues 92–105), and helix α4 (residues 111–126) (Figure 7A) – bounded by partially disordered regions at its amino and carboxy terminal boundaries.
evidence: The manuscript presents the NMR structure (Figure 7A) and describes its secondary structure elements.

claim: The PrgI-binding region of OrgC (residues 134–141) falls within an 8-residue flexible loop dangling from the 4-helix central core domain
source: The PrgI-binding region of OrgC (residues 134–141) falls within an 8-residue flexible loop that is dangling from the 4-helix central core domain of OrgC (Figure 7A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural location of the PrgI-binding region based on the NMR structure (Figure 7A).

claim: The PrgI-binding region of OrgC is mostly electronegative
source: Further analysis of the electrostatic surface of OrgC indicated that the PrgI-binding region is mostly electronegative (Figure 7B).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrostatic surface analysis (Figure 7B) of the OrgC structure.

claim: The corresponding surface in PrgI involved in OrgC binding is mostly electropositive
source: The corresponding surface in PrgI involved in OrgC binding is mostly electropositive (Figure 7C), suggesting a role for electrostatic interactions in the binding mechanisms.
evidence: The manuscript presents electrostatic surface analysis (Figure 7C) of PrgI and infers the role of electrostatic interactions.

claim: A database search using DALI detected no structural homologs for OrgC
source: A database search for related structures using DALI (Holm and Sander, 1993) detected no structural homologs, thus suggesting that OrgC represent a unique fold.
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of a DALI database search and cites the method (Holm and Sander, 1993).

claim: The D1 domain of the flagellar capping protein FliD loosely shares some topological features with the OrgC central four-helix domain
source: However, it is noteworthy that the D1 domain of the flagellar capping protein FliD loosely shares some of the topological features of the OrgC central four-helix domain (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript presents a topological comparison (Figure 7—figure supplement 4) between OrgC and FliD.

claim: OrgC is an 'early' substrate of the S. Typhimurium SPI-1 T3SS, co-secreted with the inner rod and needle filament proteins, and the regulatory protein InvJ
source: We found that OrgC is an 'early' substrate of the S. Typhimurium SPI-1 T3SS, co-secreted with the inner rod and needle filament proteins, and the regulatory protein InvJ.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from secretion assays showing OrgC is secreted in mutants that only secrete early substrates.

claim: OrgC may help to nucleate the initial polymerization of PrgI monomers
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that OrgC may help to nucleate the initial polymerization of PrgI monomers.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis based on multiple experimental observations including the effect on needle number but not length.

claim: Once assembly is initiated, OrgC may be discarded
source: Once assembly is initiated, OrgC may be discarded thus explaining our inability to detect it at the tip of the growing needle filaments or as an integral component of isolated NCs.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis to explain the absence of OrgC in isolated needle complexes.

claim: The function of OrgC appears to be substantially different from another protein reported to influence needle assembly in Yersinia spp.
source: The function of OrgC appears to be substantially different from another protein reported to influence needle assembly in Yersinia spp. that may involve the control of the secretion of the needle protein (Blaylock et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript compares OrgC function to a protein in Yersinia and cites prior work (Blaylock et al., 2010).

claim: The activity of OrgC and the phenotype of the ∆orgC mutant are reminiscent of flagellar capping proteins
source: However, the activity of OrgC and the phenotype of the ∆orgC mutant are reminiscent of flagellar capping proteins, which are required for the assembly of the rod, hook, and filament, the flagellar substructures that make up the entire flagellum (Ikeda et al., 1993; Ohnishi et al., 1994; Yonekura et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript compares OrgC to flagellar capping proteins and cites prior work (Ikeda et al., 1993; Ohnishi et al., 1994; Yonekura et al., 2000).

claim: Each of the different flagellar substructures has its own specific capping protein
source: Each of the different flagellar substructures has its own specific capping protein, which control their distal growth by regulating the assembly of the different subunits at the growing tip.
evidence: The manuscript draws on established knowledge about flagellar capping proteins.

claim: Unlike capping proteins, OrgC appears to be required only for the efficient initiation of needle filament assembly but not for its elongation
source: Unlike capping proteins, OrgC appears to be required only for the efficient initiation of needle filament assembly but not for its elongation.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from observations that needles in the ∆orgC mutant are normal length but reduced in number.

claim: Unlike the capping proteins, OrgC is not essential for needle assembly
source: Furthermore, unlike the capping proteins, OrgC is not essential for needle assembly. In its absence, the number of fully assembled NC is reduced although those that assemble exhibit needle filaments that are of the same length as those of wild type.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from observations that some needles still form in the ∆orgC mutant.

claim: The central core domain of OrgC exhibits topological similarities with the D1 domain of capping proteins
source: However, the NMR structure of OrgC indicates that even though it shares no amino acid sequence similarity with capping proteins, its central core domain exhibits topological similarities with the D1 domain of capping proteins (Deane et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2007; Yonekura et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript compares the OrgC structure to capping protein structures and cites prior work (Deane et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2007; Yonekura et al., 2000).

claim: OrgC may be equivalent to capping proteins lacking the 'plate' substructure
source: Therefore it is possible that OrgC may be equivalent to capping proteins lacking the 'plate' substructure, which may explain the substantial differences in the activities of these functionally related proteins.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis based on structural and functional comparisons.

claim: The diameter of the T3SS needle is significantly smaller than the diameter of the flagellar filament (8 nm vs 20 nm)
source: The diameter of the T3SS needle is significantly smaller than the diameter of the flagellar filament (8 nm vs 20 nm), which may translate into differences in its assembly mechanism, and in turn, differences in the requirement and/or function of the accessory proteins during assembly.
evidence: The manuscript states the diameter difference and infers potential implications for assembly mechanisms.

claim: OrgC homologs appear to be absent from several T3SSs
source: In fact, OrgC homologs appear to be absent from several T3SSs, suggesting that the needle filaments of these systems may have evolved a complete independence from accessory proteins for their assembly.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from sequence analysis and proposes an evolutionary interpretation.

claim: A high degree of conservation was detected in the amino acids involved in the interaction with OrgC in needle filament proteins from T3SS that have homologs of OrgC
source: In support of this hypothesis, we detected a high degree of conservation in the amino acids involved in the interaction with OrgC in needle filament proteins from T3SS that have homologs of OrgC (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents sequence alignment data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) supporting this observation.

claim: The needle complex consists of a cylindrical base ~26 nm in diameter and ~32 nm in height anchored to the inner and outer membranes
source: The NC consists of a cylindrical base ~26 nm in diameter and ~32 nm in height, which is anchored to the inner and outer membranes through multiple ring-shaped structures, and a needle-like appendage or filament that protrudes several nanometers from the bacterial surface (Marlovits et al., 2004; Schraidt et al., 2010; Worrall et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior structural studies (Marlovits et al., 2004; Schraidt et al., 2010; Worrall et al., 2016) describing the NC dimensions.

claim: The cytoplasmic sorting platform consists of a six-pod structure 23 nm in height and 36 nm in width
source: The cytoplasmic sorting platform consists of a six-pod structure 23 nm in height and 36 nm in width, capped at one of its ends by a six-spoke, wheel-like structure, all together arranged in a cage-like assembly (Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior structural study (Hu et al., 2017) describing the sorting platform dimensions.

claim: The needle is built by addition of its single subunit at the growing tip after transiting through the central channel of the nascent filament
source: The needle is built by addition of its single subunit at the growing tip after transiting through the central channel of the nascent filament (Poyraz et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Poyraz et al., 2010) describing the needle assembly mechanism.

claim: Type III protein secretion systems are encoded by many gram-negative bacteria pathogenic or symbiotic to animals, plants, or insects
source: Type III protein secretion systems (T3SSs) are highly conserved molecular machines encoded by many gram-negative bacteria pathogenic or symbiotic to animals, plants, or insects (Galán et al., 2014; Deng et al., 2017; Notti and Stebbins, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior reviews (Galán et al., 2014; Deng et al., 2017; Notti and Stebbins, 2016) describing T3SS distribution.

claim: T3SSs are evolutionarily related to flagella, sharing many elements of the machinery
source: These systems are evolutionarily related to flagella, sharing many elements of the machinery that mediates the assembly of this complex organelle (Diepold and Armitage, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Diepold and Armitage, 2015) describing the evolutionary relationship between T3SSs and flagella.

claim: T3SS machines have evolved to deliver bacterial effector proteins into eukaryotic cells to modulate cellular functions
source: Unlike flagella, which have evolved to propel bacteria through liquid environments, T3SS machines have evolved to deliver bacterial effector proteins into eukaryotic cells to modulate cellular functions, thus shaping the functional interface between symbionts or pathogens and their hosts (Galán, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Galán, 2009) describing T3SS function.
